text: SABSA is probably the most practitioner-feeling framework you'll encounter in this course, because it was built by practitioners. Three working security architects — John Sherwood, Andrew Clark, and David Lynas — created it in the nineteen-nineties, and the SABSA Institute maintains it today. Its whole reason for existing is one idea: security architecture has to start from the business, not from the technology.

SABSA's defining rule is traceability. Encrypting a database isn't automatically good security in SABSA's world — encrypting a database because the business has a stated confidentiality requirement on that data, and this control satisfies it, is what counts as architecture. If you can't trace a control back to a real business requirement, SABSA says you haven't done architecture at all. You've just implemented a control somebody happened to like.

That traceability runs through six layers. Contextual is the business itself — its goals, its risk appetite, the attributes it needs from security. Conceptual is the architect's strategy for meeting those attributes, and Logical names the security services in architectural terms before any product gets chosen. Physical, Component, and Operational get progressively more concrete, ending with who actually runs the thing day to day. Every layer below Contextual has to trace back up to it.

Pair those six layers with six questions — what, why, how, who, where, and when — asked again at every layer, and you get the SABSA Matrix: thirty-six cells in total. You won't fill in all thirty-six for every project. What you're really borrowing is the discipline — for any control you propose, be ready to answer what it protects, why it's needed, how it works, who owns it, where it lives, and when it applies.

The artifact that makes SABSA distinctly business-driven is the Business Attributes Profile. Early in an engagement, the architect sits down with business stakeholders — not IT — and builds a plain-language list of what the business actually needs: things like regulatory compliance, customer confidence, or operational resilience. Every control downstream either serves one of those named attributes, or the profile needs revisiting first. That's also what makes SABSA land well in audits and board conversations.

SABSA starts from the business and works down. Next lesson, you'll meet TOGAF, a framework that historically starts from IT architecture practice instead — and you'll see exactly where, and how awkwardly, security has had to fit into it as a cross-cutting concern rather than a first-class domain.
